Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette: John is a 45-year-old European American male who works as a journalist. He has been married for over two decades and carries with him the heavy burden of a traumatic event that occurred during his captivity several years ago. The trauma has left deep scars both physically and mentally, and he continues to struggle daily with symptoms that have significantly impacted his life. John’s memories of captivity are vivid and recurrent, like an unwelcome film playing over and over again in his mind. He can still feel the terror that gripped him when unexpected or loud sounds would jolt him back into a state of high alert. The memory forces its way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, often without any apparent trigger. This replaying of traumatic memories is particularly distressing as it brings back the same overwhelming sense of fear he felt during captivity. The intensity of these memories has made John hyperalert to potential threats in his environment. He constantly scans for signs that might indicate danger, even when there is no real threat present. The slightest noise can send him into a state of panic, and he often reacts as if he were still in immediate danger. This hypervigilance has become a dominant feature of his daily life, affecting not only how he perceives the world but also how he interacts with it. John’s physical pain, particularly in his neck, serves as another trigger for these intrusive memories. The pain is often so intense that it brings back vivid recollections of the captivity ordeal. He has come to believe that any form of touch, even a gentle pat on the shoulder or hug from his wife, can ignite these painful memories and plunge him into a state of fear. The smell of alcohol also triggers John’s traumatic memories. This association is rooted in an incident during captivity when he was subjected to alcohol as part of his torment. Now, any whiff of alcohol serves as a stark reminder of that time, causing him to retreat from social situations where such smells might be present. His hypervigilance has led him to avoid certain environments and interactions that could potentially trigger these memories and associated physical reactions. For example, he often avoids going out with colleagues for drinks after work, which has strained his professional relationships. John's avoidance behaviors have also affected his personal life; he finds himself withdrawing from social gatherings where alcohol is present, leaving both him and his wife feeling isolated. John’s constant state of false alarms further exacerbates his hypervigilance and intrusive memories. Even when there are no actual threats present, he reacts as if danger lurks around every corner. This cycle of heightened alertness and memory replay has created a self-perpetuating loop that is increasingly difficult to break. The more frequently these triggers activate his traumatic memories, the more vigilant he becomes. John's struggles have become so intense that they are starting to interfere with his work as a journalist. His job often requires him to be in various environments where unexpected sounds and physical touch can occur. He finds himself unable to focus on his assignments due to the constant intrusion of these triggers and memories, which has led to missed deadlines and strained relationships with his editors. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer function normally without the constant fear and intrusive thoughts dominating his life. His wife had also noticed a significant change in him over the past few months, becoming increasingly concerned about his well-being and urging him to seek professional assistance. Despite these challenges, John hopes for a future where he can regain control of his life and be free from the relentless cycle of fear and trauma that has defined much of his recent existence.
